title: Effect of increasing taurine and methionine supplementation on urinary taurine excretion in a model insectivore, the giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla)

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>The giant anteater (<jats:italic>Mymercophaga tridactyla</jats:italic>) is a highly specialized insectivore for which nutrient requirements are not clearly established, making diet formulation challenging for this species. Multiple clinical reports suggest anteaters have an obligate dietary taurine (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>) requirement. Sulphur amino acid (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">SAA</jats:styled-content>) metabolism in adult anteaters was evaluated using noninvasive methods to measure<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>synthesis potential from dietary methionine (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MET</jats:styled-content>) and a basal diet containing on a dry matter (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>) basis 1.7 mg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>/kg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>and 6.9 g<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MET</jats:styled-content>/kg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>. Urinary equilibrium times for<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>excretion were determined by feeding the basal diet with or without 1.5 g/kg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>supplemental<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>(crossover design;<jats:italic>n</jats:italic> = 4). Effects of supplemental dietary<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>(1.7, 2.0, 2.4, 2.7, 3.0, 3.3 g/kg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>) or<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MET</jats:styled-content>(6.9, 9.0, 11.2 g/kg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>) on urinary<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>were evaluated (randomized block trials;<jats:italic>n</jats:italic> = 5 or 4 respectively). All urinary values (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>,<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MET</jats:styled-content>, unbound inorganic sulphate) were normalized to creatinine (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CRT</jats:styled-content>). Results indicate urinary<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>equilibrium in anteaters requires at least 2 weeks of feeding. Urinary ratio of<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>to<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CRT</jats:styled-content>(<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>:<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CRT</jats:styled-content>) increased as dietary<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>content increased from 1.7 to 3.0 g/kg<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DM</jats:styled-content>, consistent with renal homoeostatic modulation of<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>excretion. Our data indicate that<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>needs were met by<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>in the basal diet or by de novo synthesis. Supplemental<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">MET</jats:styled-content>resulted in ~five‐ to eightfold increases in urinary<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>:<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CRT</jats:styled-content>excretion, further supporting existence of mechanisms for<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">TAU</jats:styled-content>synthesis from dietary<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">SAA</jats:styled-content>in anteaters.
